newsitem.title: USA: Archer asks Clinton to revise his tax proposal.
newsitem.headline: Archer asks Clinton to revise his tax proposal.

text.p: Representative Bill Archer, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, urged President Clinton Sunday to revise his child tax credit proposals, which he said would deny tax relief to many middle-income parents.

"Your proposal in effect increases welfare spending and does so by taking tax relief out of the hands of middle-income taxpaying parents with teenage children," Archer, a Texas Republican, wrote in a letter to Clinton.
He said the parents of 11 million teenagers between the ages of 13 and 17 would be denied tax relief under Clinton's tax credit proposal.

Archer said in his letter that Clinton's child tax credit proposals would give money to "people who either pay no taxes at all or who already receive tax code benefits" through the earned income tax credit.
"Tax relief shouldn't go to people who don't pay taxes," Archer said on Fox TV's "Fox News Sunday."

Archer was the author of legislation approved Friday by the House Ways and Means Committee despite unanimous opposition from member Democrats, who said the measure favoured the rich and violated the bipartisan balanced-budget agreement by curtailing college tax breaks sought by the president.

The bill provides for $135 billion worth of tax cuts over five years. Among its main provisions, the measure would grant a tax credit of up to $500 for each child under 17 in families with incomes of up to $110,000, and reduce the top rate on capital gains for individuals from 28 percent to 20 percent.

Critics complain the child tax credit would not be available to many low- and moderate-income families who receive the earned income tax credit. It also would limit credits for families claiming a credit for child-care expenses.
Republicans have accused Democrats of wanting to turn the bill into a welfare measure by providing tax relief to the working poor and other low-income wage earners.

Partisan wrangling over the measure already has spawned concerns Congress could be on a collision course with the White House over how to parcel out reductions agreed under the balanced budget plan. The House tax bill will ultimately have to be reconciled with any version approved by the Senate, which will take up the issue this week.
Clinton attacked the measure Friday by saying it would penalise the working poor and working mothers. But White House officials have avoided explicit veto threats.
